title: Hash Maps and Sets
summary: How to turn a slow search into a fast lookup by remembering what you have already seen.
keyPoints: A hash map stores key-value pairs and usually gives average O(1) lookup, insert, and delete.
A hash set is a hash map that only remembers keys; use it for membership questions.
The worst case is O(n) when many keys collide, but well-distributed keys make that rare.
The common interview move is to store each value as you scan so you never need to scan backwards.

complexity.note: The hash function finds the bucket.

commonMistakes: Inserting the current value before checking for its complement, which can pair an element with itself.
Using a list to test membership inside a loop, which turns O(n) into O(n²).
Forgetting that hash-map iteration order is not sorted and may differ between languages.
Storing a count when you only need a boolean, or storing an index when you only need a count.
interviewNotes: Name the exact thing you are trading: O(n) extra space for O(1) average lookups.
State that the O(1) bound is average case; collisions can make it worse.
If the input is sorted, ask whether two pointers can replace the map and save memory.

checkYourself.question: Why does a hash set make duplicate detection O(n) instead of O(n²)?
checkYourself.answer: Each value is checked and inserted in average O(1), so one pass over n values is O(n). A list membership check is O(n), making the nested work O(n²).

checkYourself.question: What does a hash function do?
checkYourself.answer: It converts a key into a bucket index, so the table can jump close to the key's location instead of scanning every entry.

checkYourself.question: When is a hash map the wrong choice?
checkYourself.answer: When you need sorted order, range queries, or very tight memory. A sorted array, tree, or two-pointer approach may fit better.
